column1: What is a 'datablock' in Blender's data model?
column2: A self-contained runtime unit of data with a unique name, reference count, and type signature (e.g. mesh, material, camera) that exists in memory and can reference other datablocks.

column1: What structure does Blender use to determine which datablocks must be recalculated when a property changes, and in what order?
column2: The dependency graph (a directed acyclic graph of datablock relationships), evaluated in topological order; circular references cause a cyclic dependency error.

column1: What is BMesh and what four components does it store?
column2: BMesh (Boundary Mesh) is Blender's internal half-edge mesh representation used for editing and the modifier pipeline; it stores vertices, edges, faces, and loops (directed half-edges recording which edges belong to which faces).

column1: What is the distinction between topology and geometry in mesh theory?
column2: Topology is the combinatorial structure (how vertices/edges/faces connect); geometry is the spatial coordinates of vertices. You can change one without changing the other.
A mesh where every edge is shared by exactly two faces and every vertex is surrounded by a single continuous loop of faces (no non-manifold edges/vertices).

column1: What is a BSDF and why does Blender's PBR system use it instead of arbitrary parameters?
column2: A Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function describes the probability of light scattering from an incoming direction to an outgoing direction; PBR workflows describe physical properties (roughness, metallic, etc.) and let the renderer compute appearance, ensuring consistency across lighting conditions.

column1: In Blender's FCurve system, what four points define a cubic Bezier interpolation segment between two keyframes?
column2: The two keyframe values (P0, P1) acting as endpoints, and two handle positions (H0, H1) that bend the curve, combined via P(t) = (1-t)³P0 + 3(1-t)²t·H0 + 3(1-t)t²·H1 + t³P1.

column1: What does pulling the right handle of a keyframe upward (extending the tangent) produce in animation interpolation?
column2: Ease-out deceleration — the motion slows as it leaves that keyframe.

column1: What is the rendering equation, and why can't it be solved analytically for complex scenes?
column2: Kajiya's rendering equation expresses outgoing radiance as emitted radiance plus the integral of incoming radiance times the BRDF over the hemisphere; indirect bounces create recursive nested integrals with no closed-form solution, requiring numerical approximation.

column1: What are the two fundamentally different rendering paradigms Blender implements, and which engine uses each?
column2: Path tracing (Monte Carlo simulation of photon paths) used by Cycles, and rasterization (projecting geometry with precomputed lighting approximations) used by Eevee.

column1: Why does increasing sample count reduce noise in a Cycles render?
column2: Cycles is a Monte Carlo path tracer; final pixel intensity is the mean of sampled radiance values, and by the law of large numbers, more samples cause random statistical fluctuations (noise) to average out and converge toward the correct solution.

column1: Why do physics simulations in Blender (cloth, rigid body, fluid) use discrete timestep integration instead of solving continuous differential equations directly?
column2: Computers cannot perform calculus directly; they discretize time into frames/substeps and approximate Newtonian motion (F=ma) iteratively, trading absolute accuracy for computational tractability and perceptual plausibility.
